speaker: Sandy
text: Thanks for making the time, Pat. Before we get into numbers, can you walk me through how you see where things stand?

speaker: Pat
text: Honestly? I'm looking at an invoice for a hundred and eighty thousand dollars for work I never signed off on. That's how I see it.

speaker: Sandy
text: So your position is that the change order isn't valid because you personally didn't sign it.

speaker: Pat
text: Alex had no authority to approve a change of that size. Read the contract: anything over fifty thousand needs my signature.

speaker: Sandy
text: Alex is your project manager. He signed it on your letterhead while I was on vacation, and my foreman did the work in good faith.

speaker: Pat
text: If you'd been reachable, none of this would have happened.

speaker: Sandy
text: I hear that you're frustrated, and I'd be too. Can we set aside who should have been reachable and look at what we do now?

speaker: Pat
text: Fine. But I want you to understand my situation: the bank pulled our credit line last month. I don't have a hundred and eighty thousand in cash. I don't have half that.

speaker: Sandy
text: Why did the bank pull the line?

speaker: Pat
text: Two of our tenants defaulted in the same quarter. It's temporary, but the timing is brutal.

speaker: Sandy
text: Okay, so cash is tight for at least this quarter. Here's my constraint: I have a supplier payment of ninety thousand due in fifteen days, and that invoice is what was supposed to cover it.

speaker: Pat
text: Is there any flexibility on that date, or is fifteen days hard?

speaker: Sandy
text: It's hard. Miss it and they put me on cash-on-delivery for every job I have running. That would sink me faster than it sinks you.

speaker: Pat
text: Look, I could just let you sue me over the change order and tie it up for two years. My lawyer says Alex's signature won't hold.

speaker: Sandy
text: You could. And I could file a lien on the building tomorrow, and your other tenants would love reading about that. But neither of us wants that, do we?

speaker: Pat
text: No. We don't. So what would actually work for you? What matters most: getting the full amount, or getting the supplier paid on time?

speaker: Sandy
text: The supplier, honestly. If ninety goes out in fifteen days, the rest can wait. And you still own that lakefront lot on Route 9, right? I've been...

speaker: Pat
text: The lakefront lot? You want the lot?

speaker: Sandy
text: I've wanted it for years, you know that. Say you pay ninety in cash within fifteen days and we settle the remaining ninety against the lot, at whatever an appraiser says it's worth. Does that sound like something you could live with?

speaker: Pat
text: So, to make sure I've got this: ninety in cash in fifteen days, which I can stretch to; the balance against the Route 9 lot at appraisal; and the change order dispute goes away. Have I got that right?
